n35429.title: C0 chart-boundary invariance
n35429.content:
\begin{definition}[C0 chart-boundary invariance]
\label{moise:def:chart_boundary_invariant}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.ChartBoundaryInvariant, LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.chartBoundaryInvariant_of_invarianceOfDomain}
\leanok
The chart-extraction interface says that a mathlib manifold-boundary point
lying in any preferred half-plane chart is sent by that chart to the frontier of
the chart's extended target.  At regularity $C^0$ this is proved from planar
no-retraction, Brouwer's fixed-point theorem, and invariance of domain.  The
typeclass keeps the low-level dependency modular, while
\texttt{chartBoundaryInvariant\_of\_invarianceOfDomain} supplies it
unconditionally.  This class records the boundary-to-frontier implication;
the chart-extraction layer below combines it with the reverse any-chart
characterization to obtain a boundary-faithful chart.
\end{definition}

n35430.title: Lean Eval compact surface with boundary

n35431.title: Geometric realization of a face family
n35431.content:
\begin{definition}[Geometric realization of a face family]
\label{moise:def:geometric_realization}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.GeometricRealization,
LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.GeometricFace}
\leanok
For a finite vertex type $V$ and a family $F$ of three-element vertex sets, the
realization is the set of points of the standard simplex
$\Delta^V\subseteq V\to\mathbb R$ supported on some face of $F$: the finite
union of the geometric $2$-simplexes of $F$, glued along shared barycentric
faces.  The executable anchor
\texttt{GeometricFace.inter} proves that two such faces intersect in exactly
their common barycentric face.  The realization is compact and Hausdorff by
construction.
\end{definition}

n35432.title: Geometric triangulation
n35432.content:
\begin{definition}[Geometric triangulation]
\label{moise:def:geometric_triangulation}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.GeometricTriangulation,
LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.nonempty_geometricTriangulation_iff_explicit}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:geometric_realization}
A \emph{geometric triangulation} of a space $S$ is a finite face family
together with a homeomorphism from its geometric realization onto $S$.  There
is no independent realization field: the realization is computed from the
combinatorial data, so the definition cannot be satisfied by degenerate
witnesses.  Executable anchors: the standard $2$-simplex triangulates itself,
nonempty targets force a nonempty face family with at least three vertices,
and $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb Q$ admit no geometric triangulation
(\texttt{Moise/Countermodels.lean}).
\end{definition}

n35433.title: Triangulated spaces are compact Hausdorff

n35435.title: Bordered Rad\'o triangulation; after Moise Ch.~8, Thm.~3

n35437.title: Finite simplicial complex in the plane
n35437.content:
\begin{definition}[Finite simplicial complex in the plane]
\label{moise:def:plane_complex}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.PlaneComplex}
\leanok
A \emph{plane complex} is a finite family of affine simplexes of dimension at
most two in $\mathbb R^2$: vertex positions are actual points, each face is
affinely independent, faces are closed under nonempty subsets, and any two face
carriers (convex hulls) intersect exactly in the carrier of their shared
vertices.  The support is defined as the union of the face carriers and is
compact.  Executable anchor: the closed standard triangle with its seven faces
(\texttt{Moise/Anchors.lean}).
\end{definition}

n35451.title: Jordan curve theorem for polygons; Moise Ch.~2, Thms.~1, 5, 6

n35452.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
The crossing-index argument, boundedness distinction, visibility segment to
the strip, and the global assembly from a two-gate strip are formalized.  The
explicit strip is also constructed: quantitative vertex balls and isolated
central edge rectangles cover the polygon, and its punctured part decomposes
into local sectors and half-rectangles.  Explicit rotated points prove the
four endpoint overlaps for each edge.  A finite cyclic graph argument makes
the two resulting bands path-connected, while closure of the parameter
rectangles proves that both bands approach every point of the polygon.  These
data instantiate \texttt{TwoGateStrip}; the crossing index and the
visibility-to-strip lemma then give exactly two complementary components,
their bounded/unbounded distinction, and both frontier equalities.
\end{proof}

n35453.title: Interior, exterior, closed region

n35454.title: Polygonal disks are polyhedra; Moise Ch.~2, Thm.~2

n35455.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Place the compact closed region in a large triangle, subdivide that triangle
successively by the finitely many affine lines through the polygon's edges, and
retain the chambers on the bounded side of polygonal Jordan.  Each chamber
interior misses the polygon because it lies on one closed side of every cutting
line.  The resulting finite submesh has support exactly the closed region.
\end{proof}

Approximate on the one-skeleton by \ref{moise:thm:one_skeleton_approx}, extend
across each $2$-cell by the combinatorial Schoenflies theorem
(\ref{moise:thm:cone_extension}, via \ref{moise:thm:polygonal_schoenflies_rel}),

A bounded Tietze extension of the boundary displacement and no-retraction

glue to the required PL embedding.
\end{proof}

n35478.title: The Rad\'o invariant
n35478.content:
\begin{definition}[The Rad\'o invariant]
\label{moise:def:rado_invariant}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.RadoInvariant}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:partial_triangulation}
The invariant carried through the bordered induction records that every edge
lies in at most two faces, every triangle meets the ambient manifold boundary
in one exposed simplicial face, and the absorbed region lies in the
topological interior of the support as a subset of the ambient surface.  This
includes genuine boundary points of half-disk cores.  It does not assert
connected vertex links or call the intermediate support a combinatorial
manifold; after the final support is all of the surface, the realization
homeomorphism supplies the topological surface conclusion directly.  The
empty partial triangulation satisfies the invariant for the empty region.
\end{definition}

n35479.title: Faithful intrinsic fine subdivision

n35480.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Construct the midpoint complex with old vertices and one vertex for each old
edge.  Explicit barycentric recovery proves that its affine evaluation is a
homeomorphism onto the old realization.  Corner and central triangles have at
most half the old diameter; iterate.
\end{proof}

n35481.title: Finite compact collar

n35483.title: Vanishing-error frontier glue
n35483.content:
\begin{lemma}[Vanishing-error frontier glue]
\label{moise:lem:frontier_glue}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.continuous_frontierGlue,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.continuous_frontierGlue_of_matches,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.isEmbedding_frontierGlue_of_matches}
\leanok
If a continuous map is replaced on an open set by a continuous approximation
whose error tends to zero at the frontier, the replacement and the unchanged
map glue to a continuous global map.  Distance to the complement is strongly
positive on compact subsets of the open set and gives a canonical
frontier-vanishing control.  The topology-only
\texttt{MatchesAtFrontier} form is the one used by the chart straightening,
and injectivity plus cross-image disjointness upgrades the paste to an
embedding.
\end{lemma}

n35485.title: Frontier-controlled chart straightening
n35485.content:
\begin{theorem}[Frontier-controlled chart straightening]
\label{moise:thm:controlled_chart_straightening}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.IntrinsicTwoComplex.RegionControlledAdaptiveComplex.exists_polygonalReplacement_of_comparison,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.PartialTriangulation.exists_straightenedChartOpen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.PartialTriangulation.exists_straightenedChartAway,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.Moise.PartialTriangulation.exists_boundaryPreservingStraightening}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:boundary_faithful,moise:thm:cone_extension,
  moise:thm:polygonal_schoenflies_rel,moise:lem:frontier_glue}
On an open chart overlap, an adaptive locally finite subdivision supports a
cellwise polygonal replacement within any strongly positive error control.
Shrinking the control toward the overlap frontier makes the replacement match
the old embedding there.  It stays in the permitted chart region, is disjoint
from the unchanged outside image, and preserves the half-plane boundary
stratum.  Consequently it pastes to a boundary-preserving embedding of the old
intrinsic complex.
\end{theorem}

n35486.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Choose an adaptive open cover subordinate to the pointwise error and target
region controls.  Polygonalize its locally finite one-skeleton, fill every
face using the polygonal Schoenflies/cone-extension construction, and use the
facewise comparison separation to obtain a compatible homeomorphism of
supports.  The vanishing error gives
\texttt{MatchesAtFrontier}; \ref{moise:lem:frontier_glue} then pastes the
replacement to the unchanged embedding.  Boundary-face regularity and the
coordinate-zero preservation theorem give the boundary-stratum equivalence.
\end{proof}

n35487.title: Gluing along a common presentation; Moise Thm.~7.6

n35488.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
The realization of the union family is the set-union of the two realizations,
so the glued embedding is the two-sided paste; it is injective by the exact
agreement hypotheses, continuous because each side's preimage of a closed set
is a compact inclusion image, and an embedding as a continuous injection from
a compact realization into a Hausdorff surface.
\end{proof}

n35489.title: Crossing-case welding; Moise Ch.~8, Thm.~3 preparation

n35490.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Straighten the old complex over the chart overlap by the locally finite
controlled polygonal replacement with tolerance vanishing at the overlap
frontier, refine the straightened trace and the fixed patch complex to a
common plane subdivision (Moise's conditions (a)--(h)), and read off the
welded presentation.  The finite compact-collar theorem must not be silently
substituted for the vanishing-tolerance construction.
\end{proof}

n35491.title: The induction step; Moise Ch.~8, Thm.~3, step

n35492.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
If the new core already lies in the interior of the built support, absorb it
directly; if the absorbed region lies inside the chart patch, replace the
built complex by the patch.  In the remaining crossing case, apply the welding
theorem and glue the two presentations by \ref{moise:thm:partial_glue}; the
invariant for the union follows from the welding conclusions.
\end{proof}

n35493.title: Assembled Rad\'o induction

n35494.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Starting from the empty complex, absorb the finitely many chart cores one at a
time by \ref{moise:thm:induction_step}; when all cores are absorbed the
invariant forces the support to be everything, and a fully covering partial
triangulation is a geometric triangulation.
\end{proof}

n35500.title: Polygonal pre-realization and gluing relation

n35501.title: Polygonal occurrence adapter
n35501.content:
\begin{definition}[Polygonal occurrence adapter]
\label{moise:def:polygonal_occurrence_adapter}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.PolygonCell,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.SurfaceCellComplex.OccurrencePairingValid,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.SurfaceCellComplex.polygonalIdentifications,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.SurfaceCellComplex.PolygonalRealization}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:surface_cell_complex}
Replace every face by an indexed closed disc and every boundary occurrence by
a labelled side. The identification set consists of all ordered pairs of
distinct non-boundary occurrences whose darts are equal or inverse according
to the parameter direction. The polygonal realization is the quotient by the
equivalence relation generated by those compatible pairings. This construction
is the topological realization of the finite incidence presentation.
\end{definition}

n35505.title: Elementary moves preserve realization

n35506.content:

\leanok
The P1 realization theorem reparametrizes a subdivided boundary side.  The P2
realization theorems split a polygon along the new diagonal, including the
degenerate and exceptional sphere cases.  Signed presentation isomorphisms and
independent face reversals act by quotient congruence.  Induction over
\texttt{NormalizationEquivalent} composes these homeomorphisms.
\end{proof}

n35507.title: Eval quotient representatives

n35508.title: One-face carrier and quotient bridge
n35508.content:
\begin{lemma}[One-face carrier and quotient bridge]
\label{moise:lem:representative_carrier_bridge}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.SurfaceCellComplex.oneFacePolygonalPreRealizationHomeomorph,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.SurfaceCellComplex.oneFacePolygonalPreRealizationHomeomorph_sidePoint,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.quotEqvGenHomeomorph,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.eqvGenQuotientCongrRawOfGeneratorMaps}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:polygonal_occurrence_adapter,
  moise:def:eval_quotient_representatives}
Every one-face polygonal pre-realization is homeomorphic to the exact closed
unit disc used by the benchmark. A side occurrence at index $i$ and parameter
$t$ maps to the boundary coordinate $(i+t)/m$. A raw-relation quotient is
homeomorphic to the quotient by its equivalence closure, and generator maps in
both directions therefore suffice to descend the carrier homeomorphism.
\end{lemma}

n35510.title: One-face pairing-position characterization

n35512.title: Canonical normal-form incidence presentations
n35512.content:
\begin{definition}[Canonical normal-form incidence presentations]
\label{moise:def:canonical_normal_form_complexes}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableBoundaryWord,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableBoundaryWord,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableHandlePosition,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableBoundaryPosition,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableCrosscapPosition,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableBoundaryPosition,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalCellComplex,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalCellComplex_isSurfaceValid,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalCellComplex_isConnected}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:surface_cell_complex,moise:def:eval_quotient_representatives,
  moise:def:polygonal_occurrence_adapter}
The orientable word concatenates commutator blocks
$a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ and boundary blocks $c_jh_jc_j^{-1}$; the
nonorientable word uses square blocks $a_i a_i$ and the same boundary blocks.
Their lengths are $4p+3n$ and $2p+3n$. Every seam, handle, or crosscap edge
occurs twice, while each boundary-contour edge occurs once, so the resulting
one-face incidence presentations are valid and connected. Under the Eval
admissibility bounds the words are nonempty and have certified occurrence
pairings for the polygonal quotient adapter. Forward block-position maps and
exact \texttt{List.get} theorems locate every signed entry of each named
handle, crosscap, and boundary block. They do not exhaust or classify an
arbitrary finite position in either word. The sphere uses its separate
two-monogon incidence presentation.
\end{definition}

n35513.title: Canonical nonorientable pairing classification

n35514.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Use the exact occurrence finsets supplied by the canonical block positions.
The two crosscap occurrences carry equal signed darts, the two seam
occurrences carry inverse signed darts, and the singleton free occurrence
contradicts the required distinctness of a pairing.
\end{proof}

n35515.title: Canonical orientable pairing classification

n35517.title: Canonical carrier coordinates and forward generator inclusions
n35517.content:
\begin{lemma}[Canonical carrier coordinates and forward generator inclusions]
\label{moise:lem:canonical_forward_generator_coordinates}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableCarrier_handle_a_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableCarrier_handle_b_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableCarrier_boundary_c_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableCarrier_crosscap_a_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableCarrier_boundary_c_eqvGen}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:canonical_normal_form_complexes,
  moise:lem:representative_carrier_bridge}
The closed-disc carrier sends each explicit handle, crosscap, and boundary-seam
pairing into the equivalence closure of its trusted Eval relation.  For a
boundary block, canonical index $j$ corresponds to trusted index
$\operatorname{rev}(j)$; integral-period invariance reconciles the canonical
positive coordinate with the benchmark's negative angle.
\end{lemma}

n35518.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Substitute the certified block positions into the generic side-coordinate
formula.  Handle and crosscap formulas reduce by ring normalization.  For
boundary seams, use $\operatorname{rev}(j)=n-j-1$, add one full turn, and use
symmetry because the trusted generator runs from the negative to the positive
occurrence.
\end{proof}

n35519.title: Canonical generator-closure comparison
n35519.content:
\begin{lemma}[Canonical generator-closure comparison]
\label{moise:lem:canonical_generator_comparison}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableGenerator_to_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableGenerator_to_eqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientableRel_to_polygonEqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientableRel_to_polygonEqvGen,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.orientablePolygonalRealizationHomeomorph,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.nonOrientablePolygonalRealizationHomeomorph}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:canonical_normal_form_complexes,
  moise:lem:representative_carrier_bridge,
  moise:lem:one_face_pairing_positions,
  moise:lem:canonical_nonorientable_pairings,
  moise:lem:canonical_orientable_pairings,
  moise:lem:canonical_forward_generator_coordinates}
The polygonal generators of the canonical orientable and nonorientable words
generate exactly the equivalence closures of \texttt{OrientableRel} and
\texttt{NonOrientableRel} under the carrier homeomorphism.  Consequently their
polygonal realizations are homeomorphic to the corresponding Eval quotients.
\end{lemma}

n35520.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Use the exhaustive pairing classifications to package the forward coordinate
lemmas for an arbitrary polygon generator.  For the reverse direction,
case-split each trusted relation constructor and construct the corresponding
polygonal pairing.  Apply
\texttt{eqvGenQuotientCongrRawOfGeneratorMaps} to the two generator maps.
\end{proof}

n35521.title: Certified finite-cyclic normalization result

n35522.title: Faithful finite-cyclic normal-form reduction

n35523.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Following Gallier--Xu Ch.~6, remove inverse pairs, reduce vertices, merge
faces, introduce crosscaps and handles, convert mixed words to all-crosscap
form, and group boundary loops. Each elementary step preserves the faithful
polygonal realization, and the terminal word is signed-isomorphic to the
existing canonical presentation.
\end{proof}

n35524.title: Canonical endpoint realization homeomorphisms
n35524.content:
\begin{lemma}[Canonical endpoint realization homeomorphisms]
\label{moise:lem:canonical_endpoint_realizations}
\lean{LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalSphereRealizationHomeomorph,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalOrientableRealizationHomeomorph,
  LeanEval.Topology.ClassificationOfSurfaces.NormalForm.canonicalNonOrientableRealizationHomeomorph}
\leanok
\uses{moise:def:eval_quotient_representatives,
  moise:def:canonical_normal_form_complexes,
  moise:lem:canonical_generator_comparison}
Each admissible canonical finite-cyclic presentation realizes the exact
corresponding Eval target: the separate two-monogon presentation realizes the
sphere, while the orientable and nonorientable one-face words realize the two
vendored quotient relations.
\end{lemma}

n35525.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
For the sphere, identify the two monogons with the two hemispheres and descend
the boundary gluing.  For the other branches, enumerate the typed canonical
one-face word and compose that quotient congruence with
\ref{moise:lem:canonical_generator_comparison}.
\end{proof}
